children: Agora, a recently founded healthcare investment firm, has closed its first deal, investing $47 million in data and analytics company Vheda Health.
San Francisco-based Agora plans to announce the deal Thursday. Terms of the transaction weren't disclosed.

The investment marks the first institutional money Vheda has received since its founding in 2013. The Columbia, Md.-based company's data and analytics systems allow health plans to identify high-risk patients and intervene to improve health outcomes and save money.
Agora was founded earlier this year by Neil Vangala, formerly a managing director at Miami-based healthcare investment firm Eir Partners.
Vheda will continue to be led by Shameet Luhar, a co-founder and its chief executive. The company plans to use the cash infusion to expand geographically, develop new products and make acquisitions.
Agora's goal is "to back and build companies that take costs out of the healthcare system," said Vangala, the firm's managing partner.

The Vheda acquisition fits squarely with that objective, Vangala said. The company's platform focuses on patients with chronic conditions and those who need maternal care, two drivers of healthcare costs in the U.S. The company says it has generated more than $975 million in savings for the health plans it works with.

Agora's strategy is to invest in healthcare information-technology and life-sciences technology companies that are either founder-owned or backed by venture capital, and operating in end markets that are growing at about three times the rate of the U.S. gross domestic product, Vangala said. It targets equity investments of $30 million to $60 million.

Agora is in the process of raising its debut fund, with the assistance of advisory firm Rede Partners, according to a May filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing doesn't list a target size for the Agora Partners Capital Fund I.
Vangala declined to comment on fundraising.
Private-equity healthcare investments surged last year, reaching a record $182 billion in global deal value, according to consulting firm Bain & Co.

In the first half of this year, however, activity declined, as macroeconomic pressures from war in the Middle East, stress in the private-credit market and turmoil in the software sector reduced dealmaking.

Globally, there were 184 deals valued at a collective $51 billion in this year's first half, Bain said. Deal activity in the healthcare IT sector was particularly muted, and investors have been cautious about putting their assets up for sale on the market, Bain said.

Vangala said he isn't overly concerned about recent issues affecting the healthcare IT sector, and he has confidence in its long-term prospects. He expects the effort to reduce costs in the healthcare system to continue over the next several decades, with providers and insurers under systemic pressure to keep expenses low.
